summary: A 1970 note on flow control, comparing fixed allocation with demand allocation of resources between hosts. Flow control stops a sender from overwhelming a receiver.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 59 compares reserving buffer space in advance with asking senders to pause only when a receiver needs room. The author favors demand allocation because it uses resources more flexibly, while acknowledging that extreme bursts can still fill buffers.

questions: flow control fixed versus demand allocation
how does cease on link flow control work
subtitle: A comparison of fixed buffer reservations and demand-based flow control.

tldr.problem: A receiver needs protection from incoming data it cannot process, but reserving buffer space for every link can waste resources and limit transmission.
tldr.mechanism: The note compares advance buffer allocation with demand allocation, where a receiver asks a sender to cease on a link when its input queue grows too large and later sends a resume command.
tldr.outcome: The author prefers demand allocation for its flexibility and lower normal-operation overhead, while acknowledging a risk of temporary buffer overload.

facts.label: Fixed-allocation safety condition
facts.value: No more than 100% of NCP buffer space allocated

today: The unit metadata records RFC 59 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document compares flow-control proposals and states the author's preference for demand allocation.

sections.title: Fixed Allocation Reserves Space in Advance
sections.content:
The fixed-allocation method described in RFC 54 reserves buffer space before data is sent. If no more than 100% of an NCP's buffer space is allocated, the receiver should not be presented with more messages than it can handle.

The author lists drawbacks: buffers can sit unused, allocations restrict bandwidth, requests create overhead, and allocations cannot be freely reduced when network load increases. Differences in message padding can also make sending and receiving hosts disagree about how much space has been used.
sections.plainLanguage: Fixed allocation promises buffer space to each connection before data arrives. This can protect the receiver, but reserved space may sit unused and cannot easily be reassigned when conditions change.

sections.title: Demand Allocation Uses Cease and Resume
sections.content:
With demand allocation, the receiver watches each input queue in relation to the free buffer space. If a queue becomes too large, its NCP sends a cease on link message to the IMP. The next message is still delivered, but its RFNM carries a special bit that tells the sending NCP to stop; the sender confirms suspension with an SPD message.

When the receiving process reduces its queue, the receiver sends an RSM resume message to restart sending. Flow control is applied when needed rather than through advance allocations on every connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver watches how much data is waiting. If a queue grows too large, it tells the sender to pause and later sends a resume message when space is available.

sections.title: Why the Author Prefers Demand Allocation
sections.content:
The author argues that demand allocation can use buffers more fully, allow more bandwidth, adapt to changing load and avoid routine allocation messages. The argument assumes that most links usually have little or no data waiting, while traffic and load vary.

The author acknowledges that a cease message may not stop traffic before all buffers fill during an extreme burst. The NCP may then have to stop accepting messages temporarily; in a severe continuing case, it may delete the input queue for the worst offending link to resume communication.
sections.plainLanguage: Demand allocation avoids reserving space when it is not needed. It can still face temporary overload if data arrives faster than the receiver can process it.

sections.title: The Trade-off in the Proposal
sections.content:
RFC 59 recommends the cease-on-link demand approach over fixed allocation. Its main claimed benefits are better resource use, more flexibility, less routine overhead and fewer restrictions on transmission.

Its stated drawback is the possibility of temporary overload under extreme conditions. The author considers this preferable to the costs of fixed allocation.
sections.plainLanguage: The author favors pausing a sender only when the receiver needs room. This uses resources more flexibly, though it cannot prevent every temporary overload.
